thread.title_full: Legislature considering bill to protect groundwater resources

author: ohtadmin
title: Legislature considering bill to protect groundwater resources
text:
Jamestown state Sen. Dawn Euer is co-sponsoring legislation to protect groundwater resources from overuse and overdevelopment.
The bill was introduced by Euer’s colleague, Sen. Victoria Gu, who represents the coastal towns of Westerly, Charlestown and South Kingstown. She used Jamestown as an example for crafting the legislation.
“Some wells and public water systems in parts of Rhode Island are already showing signs of stress,” Gu said. “Homeowners in Jamestown have faced failing wells and a public water system that officials are worried is reaching its limits. Especially in coastal neighborhoods that were overbuilt before zoning laws existed, it is important that continued development doesn’t stress groundwater resources beyond their capacity.”
Municipalities whose low- or moderate-income housing units comprise less than 10% of their year-round supply, like Jamestown, which is below 5%, must provide density bonuses beyond the zoned density of the property for projects that contain at least 25% affordable units.
The bonuses vary based on the percentage of affordable units in the development and whether the property is connected to public utilities or using wells and septic systems. The development still needs to pass all environment regulations for the total planned density, including the bonus units.
Wetlands, easements, rights-of-way and land needed for road infrastructure already are excluded from these bonuses.
Gu’s bill would exclude public drinking watersheds and areas classified by the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management as important public groundwater resources from these density bonuses. These groundwater resource areas, which are designated as “GAA,” include aquifers, wellhead protection and dependent areas that are physically isolated from alternative water supplies.
These areas make up about 21% of Rhode Island.
The bill also would ensure that to be eligible for these density bonuses, properties would not only have to have access to either public water or a private well, as the law currently requires, but also the applicable water system must have the capacity to support the proposed density of the project.
About two-thirds of Rhode Island’s municipalities rely on groundwater as a significant source of drinking water. State environmental officials consider the groundwater resources vulnerable to contamination due to their generally shallow depth and permeability to outside contaminates.
Rep. Megan Cotter, who serves Exeter, Richmond and Hopkinton, has introduced companion legislation in the House.
“Rhode Island is in a housing crisis and it’s important for every community to do its part to solve it,” she said. “However, it would be short-sighted and counterproductive to allow housing development to put at risk the groundwater resources that supply drinking water across the state. This bill will keep affordable housing incentives intact while ensuring that the clean groundwater that keeps Rhode Island green and livable is protected.”
